sections.text:
Запрос:
I am finalizing the stable 1.0 database schema and public API of an open-source Laravel "drive" package (folders, files with revisions on content-addressed blobs, collaborative documents, multi-tenant hosts). Compare with official documentation of Google Drive API v3, Box API, Dropbox API, Microsoft Graph (OneDrive/SharePoint driveItem), Nextcloud/WebDAV, Amazon S3. Cite docs; mark undocumented points. Give a concrete recommendation per topic and a final table "field/rule | vendors | recommendation | risk if wrong".

1. Identifiers: do these APIs expose opaque string IDs rather than sequential integers? Why (enumeration, sharding, merges, migrations)? Should a library whose host may choose bigint/ULID/UUID primary keys expose a separate stable opaque public id, or is an unguessable ULID/UUID PK enough? Effects of exposing sequential bigint ids even with authorization (existence oracle, timing).
2. Names: max length (bytes vs characters), Unicode normalization (NFC/NFD, macOS), case-insensitive uniqueness but case-preserving, forbidden characters (/, \, NUL, control chars), trailing dots/spaces (Windows), reserved names (CON, PRN, desktop.ini), leading/trailing whitespace trimming. What do Drive (allows duplicates!), Box (unique per folder, 255 chars), Dropbox (case-insensitive paths), OneDrive (forbidden chars list, 400 char path) do? Recommended rule set for a portable library that must sync with desktop OSes and export ZIPs.
3. Tree constraints: single parent vs multiple parents (Drive's 2020 move to single-parent + shortcuts), max depth, max items per folder, shortcuts semantics (target deleted, permissions of target), moving across drives/tenants.
4. Timestamps and attribution: created_at, modified_at (metadata), content_modified_at (Box content_modified_at, Drive modifiedTime vs modifiedByMeTime), last modifying user, client-provided original timestamps on upload (Dropbox client_modified vs server_modified, Box content_created_at). Which belong in a stable schema?
5. Custom metadata: Drive properties/appProperties (limits), Box metadata templates/instances, Graph open extensions/schema extensions, S3 user metadata limits (2 KB). Recommend: public key-value "properties" with namespace + size limits vs free-form JSON column; indexing/searchability; who may write.
6. Per-user state vs shared state: Drive starred, viewedByMeTime, Box favorites/collections, Dropbox pins? Is "pinned"/"starred" a per-user relation or a node attribute? Manual ordering ("position") of folder children — supported anywhere? Recommendation.
7. Size and count limits as configuration: max file size, max folder children, max path depth, max name length, max revisions per file — what vendors publish and how to make them configurable per tenant/profile without schema changes.


Ответ:
For 1.0, I recommend a stable identity contract independent of host primary-key choice, a single-parent tenant-scoped tree, case-preserving names with a versioned portability policy, separate server and original-content timestamps, bounded namespaced metadata, and per-user favorites. Do not copy one vendor’s complete model: Google Drive permits duplicate names, Box exposes numeric-looking string IDs, Nextcloud exposes integer file IDs, and S3 is a flat object store—not a drive tree.
Below, “undocumented” means not established by the official documentation cited here—not proof that a vendor has no such behavior. Recommendations are proposed contracts for your package, not claims about vendors’ internal schemas.

## Identifiers and tree structure


## 1. Public identifiers

The reasons vendors chose particular ID formats—enumeration resistance, sharding, mergers, migration flexibility—are undocumented in these resource specifications. Those are legitimate design benefits to evaluate, but not verified explanations of vendor architecture.
Recommendation:
- Public API id: an immutable string, never a JSON number.
- Default database implementation: host-selected internal PK plus unique public_id.
- Allow public_id to reuse a UUID/ULID PK only when the host guarantees that it remains immutable and survives imports, storage migrations, and PK strategy changes.
- Do not require a second random identifier solely because the PK is already a suitable immutable UUID. The useful separation is contractual; a duplicate column is an implementation choice.
- For your embeddable library, a separate default public_id is nevertheless the safer baseline: choosing bigint internally should not silently change the external security and compatibility characteristics.
- IDs are identifiers, not bearer credentials. Public-share tokens must be separate, revocable secrets.
A correctly authorized sequential-bigint API is not automatically vulnerable to unauthorized reads. Its disadvantages are easier probing and correlation: observable 403 versus 404, error bodies, bulk lookup responses, caches, or timing differences may expose existence or activity. Random IDs reduce practical guessing but do not fix authorization or an existence oracle once an ID is known.
I would make unknown and unreadable resources return the same public 404 contract, while allowing 403 for an operation on an already readable resource. Google Drive explicitly documents 404 for either nonexistent files or files the caller cannot read. This does not promise constant-time behavior; minimize divergent lookup/authorization paths and rate-limit probing.
For UUID/ULID, avoid promising “unguessable” as a blanket property: time-ordered identifiers can disclose approximate creation time, and security depends on generation quality. Document opacity and immutability, not secrecy.

## 3. Tree constraints

Google announced the single-location transition in March 2020, with multiple-folder placement ending September 30, 2020. Current v3 documentation permits one parent; shortcuts represent additional placements.
Box exposes a singular parent. Graph exposes parentReference, and its ordinary move operation cannot move items between drives. Nextcloud exposes path-based MOVE/COPY. S3 has no real folders: prefixes only emulate hierarchy.
Google documents 100 nested folder levels for My Drive and shared drives, plus 500,000 direct children in a folder. Do not confuse a folder-child limit with a drive-wide item limit or a sync-client recommendation.
- Every non-root node has exactly one folder parent within the same tenant and drive.
- Give each drive an explicit root node. This avoids nullable-parent uniqueness problems and ambiguous top-level semantics.
- Enforce parent scope with database constraints where supported, not only Eloquent scopes.
- Prevent cycles transactionally. A preflight ancestor check without concurrency control is insufficient.
- Check the entire moved subtree against depth/path policies, not just the moved folder.
- Preserve public IDs for same-drive rename/move.
- Reject cross-tenant move in 1.0. Provide an explicit copy/import operation that creates new identities and applies destination ownership, ACL, retention, and quota policies.
- Default to rejecting cross-drive move too. If needed later, add a dedicated transfer command rather than allowing arbitrary drive_id mass assignment.
Google shortcuts do not grant target permissions. Their titles are visible in the containing location, but opening them requires access to the target; deleted, trashed, or inaccessible targets cause broken shortcuts. Deleting a shortcut does not delete its target.
If shortcuts belong in 1.0, make them a distinct node kind with their own parent/name/ACL and a target reference. Resolve target authorization on every content access; do not recursively expand shortcut folders during ordinary traversal. Preserve broken shortcuts, return a neutral “target unavailable” result, and do not expose deleted-target metadata to unauthorized callers. Same-tenant targets only is a reasonable first-version restriction.

## Portable names


## 2. Vendor behavior

“255 characters” is not interchangeable with 255 UTF-8 bytes, Unicode code points, UTF-16 units, or grapheme clusters. Box’s cited schema establishes maxLength: 255, but does not explain all supplementary-character counting or normalization details. Likewise, do not infer a vendor’s exact Unicode comparison algorithm merely from “case-insensitive.”
The macOS issue is also more nuanced than “macOS uses NFD”: Apple documents APFS as normalization-preserving but normalization-insensitive, whereas HFS+ stores a normalized form. Dropbox documents collisions between visually identical, differently encoded names, without specifying a complete normalization algorithm.

## Recommended naming contract

Use a default portable-desktop-v1 profile:
- Accept valid UTF-8 only; normalize accepted names to NFC and return the canonical name.
- Preserve case in name.
- Calculate an internal name_key = NFC(full_unicode_casefold(NFC(name))) using a specified, versioned Unicode algorithm.
- Require uniqueness across all active child kinds—folder, file, document, shortcut—within the same parent.
- Limit the canonical name to 255 UTF-8 bytes and 255 UTF-16 code units. Measure after normalization.
- Reject empty names, . and .., NUL, Unicode control characters, and < > : " / \ | ? *.
- Reject leading/trailing Unicode whitespace and trailing ASCII periods. Do not silently trim.
- Reject Windows device basenames case-insensitively, including when followed by an extension: CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1–COM9, LPT1–LPT9, and the documented superscript-digit variants. Windows documents those special device-name rules.
- For the portable profile, additionally reserve COM0, LPT0, desktop.ini, and .DS_Store. Treat these extra exclusions as policy, not universal filesystem-invalid names.
For a OneDrive-specific profile, additionally enforce .lock, ~$ prefixes, _vti_ anywhere in a name, root-level forms, and other current vendor-specific rules. OneDrive distinguishes invalid names from system files its sync client normally excludes or deletes.
Do not ban all Unicode format characters indiscriminately: some are important for legitimate scripts and emoji sequences. A separate security policy can reject bidi override/isolate controls if your UI cannot display them safely.
Example: Résumé.pdf and an equivalent decomposed spelling must conflict; Report.pdf and report.pdf must conflict; a case-only rename of the same node must succeed.
Implementation recommendations:
- Store name and a binary-compared name_key; do not delegate the public contract to whichever database collation the host happens to use.
- The folded key can be longer than the display name. Size its storage independently.
- Back uniqueness with a database constraint; handle races as a stable name_conflict error.
- Let trashed names become reusable, then make restore fail with conflict or require an explicit new name. Never silently overwrite.
- Pin the normalization/case-fold policy version. Changing it requires collision detection and a migration plan.
This is a defensible portability baseline, not a guarantee that every OS, old application, or vendor compares every Unicode character identically.
For paths, enforce profile-specific limits separately from component length. A 400-character server-relative path may satisfy OneDrive’s cloud limit yet fail on a local extraction destination. Dropbox’s guidance is stricter, and local root-directory length consumes additional budget.
For ZIP export, always validate the produced archive paths independently: relative paths only, no traversal or absolute paths, collision detection after export-name mapping, and no automatic shortcut-to-symlink conversion. Default to failure on an unrepresentable name; offer explicit deterministic renaming with a manifest when requested. Never silently replace several incompatible names with the same _-based output.

## Timestamps, metadata, and user state


## 4. Timestamps and attribution

Recommendation: avoid making content_modified_at mean both “trusted server content commit” and “original client mtime.”
If you need metadata-only time, add metadata_modified_at; do not redefine modified_at later. Keep Laravel updated_at as an implementation timestamp unless you explicitly guarantee that every database touch has public modification semantics.
Store original-content times on revisions, with the current node optionally projecting its head revision’s values. They belong neither to the shared content-addressed blob nor to its deduplication key: identical bytes may arrive from different files with different timestamps and authors.
For collaborative documents, define content_modified_at at durable persistence boundaries. A snapshot worker is not necessarily the author of the edits it snapshots; revision attribution may need a system actor plus contributor information. Personal favorites/view activity must not bump the shared resource version or shared modification timestamps.

## 5. Custom metadata

Google supports shared properties and app-private appProperties: 100 total properties per file, 30 public properties, 30 private properties per application, and 124 UTF-8 bytes for each combined key/value pair. These are much smaller than a general JSON document.
Box uses scoped metadata templates and instances, with template/version information in the file representation; its metadata permissions follow folder permissions.
Graph needs a specific correction: generic Graph extension support does not mean stable driveItem support. The v1.0 open-extension supported-resource list does not include driveItem, and schema extensions likewise do not list it. Beta documentation does list driveItem open extensions with different limits. Do not make a stable sync adapter depend on that beta capability.
S3 user metadata is limited to 2 KB, measured as combined UTF-8 key/value bytes; keys are stored lowercase, and changing it requires copying the object. It is a poor canonical store for mutable node metadata, especially when several revisions/nodes share one blob.
Recommendation: expose bounded namespaced string properties in 1.0, not arbitrary recursively typed JSON:
```
{ "properties": { "com.example.crm": { "record_id": "customer-184", "category": "contract" } } }
```
Suggested package defaults—not vendor limits:
- Namespace: registered ASCII identifier, maximum 128 bytes.
- Key: maximum 64 ASCII bytes.
- Value: UTF-8 string, maximum 1,024 bytes.
- Maximum 100 entries across namespaces.
- Maximum 16 KiB total canonical serialized properties per node.
- Explicit deletion operation; omit means unchanged, not deleted.
- Patch entries atomically with optimistic concurrency; avoid whole-object replacement as the only write operation.
Separate visibility from namespace naming. A namespace called private is not an access-control mechanism. Use explicit shared versus application-private scope, tied to the authenticated integration identity.
Who may write:
- Shared properties: actor with metadata-edit capability.
- App-private properties: that application identity plus node access and the required write capability.
- Reserved package/host namespaces: privileged system actors only.
- Retention, ACL, tenant identity, blob keys, and authoritative revision state: dedicated fields/commands, never arbitrary properties.
A JSON/JSONB column is acceptable storage behind this contract. Use a property table or explicit indexed projections only when indexed queries are required. Promise search/filtering only for registered keys; do not accidentally commit to arbitrary indexed JSON search.
Provider adapters must validate provider-specific budgets. Your 16 KiB node metadata must not be assumed exportable into Drive properties or S3 headers.

## 6. Personal versus shared state

Drive’s starred explicitly means whether the requesting user starred the file; its “by me” timestamps are also user-relative. Box collections are private to the user even when the content is shared. Nextcloud exposes favorites and user-specific favorite listing through DAV.
A Dropbox API v2 pin field or public pin-management endpoint is undocumented in the file interfaces verified here. Do not equate a Dropbox UI feature with a guaranteed API contract.
```
node_user_state tenant_id node_id actor_type actor_id starred_at nullable last_viewed_at nullable last_modified_by_me_at nullable
```
Use a unique node/actor scope. Public resource responses may include a viewer_state projection, but serialize/cache it per actor; never cache it as universally shared node metadata.
Use starred for personal preference. If “pinned” means “highlighted for everyone in this folder,” implement a separate shared placement rule requiring folder-management permission.
Manual ordering is undocumented as a persistent arbitrary child-position field in the cited mainstream resource contracts. Sorting API results is not the same thing as storing user-defined order.
For 1.0, omit position unless you have a concrete requirement. If needed:
- Personal order belongs to actor + parent + child.
- Shared order belongs to the parent-child placement and needs its own capability.
- Use an opaque rank and deterministic ID tie-breaker; do not expose contiguous integers as an invariant.
- Moving a node resets or explicitly translates its placement rank.
- Concurrent reorder requires version checking or another documented conflict policy.

## Limits and configuration


## 7. Published limits

Two especially important distinctions:
- A provider’s upload-endpoint limit may differ from its browser, sync-client, account-quota, or plan limit.
- A content-addressed package revision is not an S3 object version. Several package revisions may reference one immutable blob; do not rely on bucket versioning to implement file history.

## Recommended policy interface

Resolve a policy object at operation time from host configuration, tenant overrides, and an optional compatibility profile:
```
DrivePolicy policy_version name_policy_version max_file_bytes max_folder_children max_folder_depth max_name_utf8_bytes max_name_utf16_units max_relative_path_utf16_units max_properties_bytes max_property_count max_revisions_per_file revision_retention_days
```
Use integers in explicitly documented units. null should mean “no package policy limit,” not “the storage provider is unlimited.” For provider-integrated operations, apply all relevant restrictions; only take a numeric minimum where the units and semantics match.
Concrete baseline:
- portable-desktop-v1: the naming policy above.
- max_folder_depth = 100, with root at depth 0 and first-level folders at depth 1.
- max_folder_children = 10_000 as a conservative, overridable package operational default—not an industry standard.
- max_file_bytes: require an explicit host/storage-profile choice rather than adopting a cloud vendor’s maximum.
- max_revisions_per_file: configurable; no automatic destructive pruning by default.
- Path budget: explicitly select the target profile and local-root allowance. Do not claim universal portability from one server-relative number.
Make limits executable invariants:
- Check upload size at admission, during streaming, and at finalization; do not trust declared length.
- Serialize child-count admission on a parent lock or equivalent transactional counter.
- Validate subtree depth/path on rename/move.
- Enforce policies in import, restore, background jobs, and system-actor operations—not only HTTP controllers.
- Decreasing a limit must not delete existing data. Permit reads and remediation; reject operations that worsen the violation.
- Retention pruning must preserve head revisions and protected/held revisions, then garbage-collect blobs only when no references remain.
- Define whether trashed nodes count against operational child limits; I recommend counting them until purge to bound retained work, while releasing their live-name reservation.
- Return stable machine errors such as name_conflict, invalid_name, file_size_limit_exceeded, folder_children_limit_exceeded, tree_depth_limit_exceeded, and cross_tenant_move_forbidden, with policy/version details only where safe.
The schema needs enough storage headroom for supported policy changes. Configurability cannot make a VARCHAR(255) support an arbitrarily larger name contract without migration. Keep physical storage ceilings separate from policy limits.

## Final decision table

Sources:
1. [developers.google](https://developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/reference/rest/v3/files)
2. [developer.box](https://developer.box.com/reference/files-resources)
3. [dropbox](https://www.dropbox.com/developers/paper-api-alpha)
4. [developers.google](https://developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/guides/handle-errors)
5. [google](https://support.google.com/drive/answer/9700156?hl=en&co=GENIE.Platform=Desktop)
6. [nextcloud](https://docs.nextcloud.com/server/stable/admin_manual/configuration_files/windows_compatible_filenames.html)
7. [aws.amazon](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-keys.html)
8. [learn.microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file)
9. [microsoft](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/onedrive/restrictions-and-limitations-in-onedrive-and-sharepoint)
10. [dropboxapi](https://docs.dropboxapi.com/dropbox-api/api-reference/user-endpoints/files/restore)

sections.title: R6 — ревизии, хранение, хеши, MIME, рендиции, дедупликация, целостность
sections.text:
Запрос:
For a Laravel file-storage package (files with immutable revisions stored as content-addressed blobs with per-scope dedup and ref-counted GC; optional virus scanning; S3 or local disks), compare official docs of Google Drive API v3 (revisions, keepForever, md5Checksum/sha1Checksum/sha256Checksum, contentRestrictions), Box (file versions, version retention, representations), Dropbox (revisions, content_hash), Microsoft Graph (driveItem versions, hashes quickXorHash/sha256, thumbnails), Amazon S3 (versioning, noncurrent version expiration, additional checksums CRC32C/SHA-256 full-object vs composite, Object Lock), Nextcloud versioning (expiration algorithm). Cite docs, mark undocumented points, end with a recommendation table.

1. Revision retention: default policies (Drive 100 revisions/30 days for binary unless keepForever, max keepForever count; Nextcloud thinning schedule; S3 lifecycle NoncurrentDays/NewerNoncurrentVersions). Recommended configurable policy model (count, age, thinning, pinned) and who may delete a single revision; does deleting a revision free quota; can the head revision be deleted.
2. Checksums: which hashes to store and expose, how clients verify uploads (Content-MD5, x-amz-checksum-*, Dropbox content_hash block scheme), full-object vs multipart composite checksums, and whether to expose storage ETags. Recommendation for a stable schema.
3. MIME type: declared vs detected (sniffed) type, which one is authoritative for preview/download Content-Type, and safe download headers (Content-Disposition attachment, nosniff) to avoid stored XSS.
4. Derived renditions: thumbnails/previews/text extraction (Box representations, Graph thumbnails) — keyed by source revision/content hash, lifecycle tied to revision, storage separate from originals, regeneration/versioning of renderers. Should a 1.0 schema reserve a renditions table?
5. Content-addressed dedup security: cross-user/tenant dedup side channels (Dropbox 2011 "Dropship", confirmation-of-file attacks, client-side dedup), and recommendation: dedup scope per tenant/drive only, server-side only, never reveal "already exists". Encryption at rest per tenant/drive (envelope encryption, key rotation) interplay with dedup.
6. Integrity: periodic scrubbing/verification of stored objects, handling missing/corrupted blobs, reconciliation between DB and object storage, orphan cleanup grace periods.
7. Quota accounting: count all revisions or head only? trash counted? shared files counted to owner? Drive/Box/Dropbox behaviour and recommendation.


Ответ:
Use application-owned immutable revisions over scope-local content-addressed blobs; treat cloud versioning, retention, hashes, and previews as adapter capabilities—not your domain model. For 1.0, make SHA-256 of the complete plaintext bytes the canonical content identity, keep reference edges authoritative, and reserve a small rendition model without requiring preview/OCR implementations.
Below, “documented” means supported by the cited public documentation; “proposal” means my recommendation for your package. “Undocumented” means the reviewed docs do not establish that behavior—not that the service necessarily lacks it.

## 1. Revisions, retention, and quota


## Documented retention behavior

Nextcloud’s documented thinning schedule is unusually useful as a design reference:
Nextcloud adjusts this pattern when a new version is created. Its version store is limited to 50% of the user’s currently available free space, with oldest versions removed under pressure; the reviewed admin manual additionally says pressure cleanup preserves at least the two most recent versions. Do not translate this into “versions may consume 50% of total quota.”

## Deleting individual revisions

For your package, define permissions explicitly rather than copying an incomplete vendor role matrix:
- revision.read, revision.delete, revision.pin, revision.unpin, and file.purge are separate capabilities.
- Default revision deletion to owner/drive manager or an explicitly delegated capability—not automatically every content editor.
- Reject deletion of the current head through revision.delete. Require file trash/purge or creation of a new replacement head.
- Restore by creating a new revision pointing to the selected historical blob; preserve historical identities.
- Distinguish a user pin, which authorized users may remove, from a legal hold/minimum retention lock, which ordinary users cannot bypass.
- Retention jobs must pass through the same protection checks, with an auditable system actor.
Drive’s contentRestrictions.readOnly prevents new revisions, comment changes, and title changes; owner-restricted and system-restricted forms have distinct removal rules. It is not documented there as a WORM storage guarantee. S3 Object Lock explicitly protects object versions against deletion/overwrite for a retention period or indefinitely. Keep “read-only,” “pin,” and “legal retention” separate concepts.

## Proposed policy model

Prefer a versioned policy object over a single keep_last setting:
```
{ "policy_version": 1, "minimum_noncurrent_count": 10, "minimum_age_days": 7, "maximum_age_days": 365, "maximum_noncurrent_count": 100, "thinning": [ {"until_days": 1, "interval_seconds": 3600}, {"until_days": 30, "interval_seconds": 86400}, {"until_days": 365, "interval_seconds": 604800} ], "protect_pinned": true }
```
This is a proposal, not a vendor-equivalent policy. Specify precedence: legal hold → head → pins → minimum guarantees → thinning/count/maximum-age deletion. Reject contradictory policies, or document which guarantees win. Define whether age starts at creation or superseded_at; I recommend the latter for noncurrent retention.
A “maximum count” cannot be an unconditional hard cap if pins and minimum-age guarantees may exceed it. Expose retained-over-limit status instead of silently breaking protection.

## Quota accounting

Proposal: default to logical bytes of all retained original revisions, including trash, charged once per revision to the owning drive/tenant. Keep physical deduplicated bytes as a separate operational metric. Allow head-only billing as a host policy, but disclose—and bound—the resulting history/trash subsidy.
Deleting a revision should release its logical charge transactionally. It releases physical bytes only after the last reference disappears, the GC grace period ends, and backend deletion succeeds. Renditions, upload reservations, replicas, and S3 noncurrent objects need separate accounting categories.

## 2. Checksums and upload verification


## Documented hash contracts

For S3 multipart uploads, the relevant documented matrix is:
A composite SHA-256 is based on part digests, not directly on all object bytes; changing part boundaries can change it without changing content. S3’s at-rest Batch Operations checksum facility can compute full-object SHA-256, so “S3 cannot calculate whole-object SHA-256” would also be too broad. Upload validation and at-rest computation are different capabilities.

## Proposed stable schema

Use a canonical digest plus extensible checksum records:
```
blobs: id, scope_id, plaintext_sha256, plaintext_size, state blob_checksums: blob_id algorithm // sha256, md5, sha1, crc32c, dropbox-content-hash-v1... construction // full_object, multipart_composite, block_hash_v1 byte_domain // plaintext, stored_ciphertext digest_bytes parameters_json // block size, part count/boundaries where necessary provenance // server_computed, provider_reported, client_claimed verified_at blob_locations: blob_id, disk, object_key, provider_version_id storage_etag, storage_size, encryption_metadata
```
Proposal details:
- Enforce uniqueness on (scope_id, plaintext_sha256); do not use a globally addressable hash as an authorization credential.
- Store canonical SHA-256 as 32 binary bytes or consistently validated 64-character lowercase hex.
- Expose canonical whole-file SHA-256 and byte size after authorization.
- Make MD5/SHA-1 optional compatibility values, not required canonical columns.
- Keep client assertions separate from verified digests.
- Keep storage ETags opaque and internal by default. An application HTTP ETag may represent a revision/response, but must not promise to be the backend checksum.
S3 ETags are not generally whole-file MD5: multipart and SSE-KMS/SSE-C cases break that assumption.

## Upload verification paths

- Package-proxied upload: stream to staging while computing whole-file SHA-256; compare any client assertion before commit.
- Direct single-part S3 upload: require a signed checksum header, such as x-amz-checksum-sha256, then confirm object identity, size, and returned checksum before publishing.
- Direct multipart upload: configure the checksum algorithm at initiation, validate parts, and use full-object CRC32C for transfer integrity if appropriate; separately compute/trustworthily verify canonical whole-file SHA-256 before CAS finalization.
- Dropbox adapter: compute the documented block hash and compare it with server-returned content_hash; keep ordinary SHA-256 separate.
S3 validates supplied checksums and rejects mismatches. Content-MD5 carries a Base64 digest, as do S3 algorithm-specific checksum values; your public hex SHA-256 therefore needs explicit encoding conversion. Merely storing a claimed digest in object metadata does not validate uploaded bytes.

## 3. MIME types and renditions


## MIME authority and safe delivery

Drive attempts content detection when no MIME type is supplied; its file MIME type cannot change without uploading a new revision. That API contract does not imply that a client-supplied type is security-validated. OWASP explicitly warns that upload Content-Type is spoofable.
Proposal: retain three distinct concepts:
A sniffer can misclassify polyglots and does not sanitize HTML/SVG. Use allowlists and format-aware validation where needed; mismatch should cause rejection, quarantine, or forced download—not automatic trust in either claim.
For untrusted originals, default to:
```
Content-Type: application/octet-stream Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="document.bin"; filename*=UTF-8''document.bin X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
```
attachment requests download; nosniff prevents reinterpretation of the supplied MIME type. Neither makes intentionally served text/html safe. Sanitize filenames using a response-header builder, and serve explicitly allowed previews from an isolated origin with restrictive policy rather than the authenticated application origin.
Optional virus scanning should introduce explicit states: pending, clean, infected, error, and not_scanned. Proposal: with scanning enabled, publish/download/preview only after a clean result unless the host deliberately opts into a different policy. Record scanner and signature versions; a digest match must not bypass a required newer scan.

## Documented rendition capabilities

Box representations are alternative assets including PDFs, thumbnails, and extracted text. They can be generated on upload or demand, exposed through GET /files/:id?fields=representations and x-rep-hints. Box also documents historical-version preview support with format limitations.
Graph exposes zero or more thumbnail sets per drive item, with multiple thumbnail objects in a set. The reviewed endpoint does not establish a general historical-revision thumbnail contract. Drive exposes a thumbnail version for cache invalidation and a short-lived thumbnail URL, not a permanent original-content identifier.
Neither these endpoints nor their resource shapes establish the vendors’ internal rendition table layout, storage separation, or GC reference model.

## Reserve a rendition table?

Yes—reserve a minimal rendition resource in 1.0, with generation implemented as an optional extension. Do not make OCR, PDF conversion, or text extraction core dependencies.
Proposed identity:
```
renditions: id, scope_id, source_blob_id kind, renderer_key, renderer_version, parameters_hash output_blob_id, mime_type, status, error_code, created_at
```
For byte-only transforms, cache by source blob/hash plus renderer version and canonical parameters. Add revision context to the key when output depends on filenames, document metadata, permissions, or watermarks.
Use a separate storage prefix/disk and separate reference edges from originals. Removing one revision removes its rendition association, not a rendition still needed by another revision referencing the same source. New renderer versions create new rendition identities; never mutate an original revision to represent renderer changes. Authorization must follow the source file/revision, including extracted text and thumbnail access.

## 4. Dedup security and integrity


## Deduplication threat model

The April 2011 Dropship analysis describes a hash-first dedup mechanism that let a client learn whether another user possessed content and potentially obtain it using its hash. It also describes confirmation attacks against guessed contents of partially known documents. This is historical evidence of the failure mode, not evidence that current Dropbox operates that way.
Proposal:
- Deduplicate only within an explicit tenant/drive security scope.
- Accept all upload bytes server-side; never authorize attachment/download from a submitted hash alone.
- Never expose a cross-scope existence probe, “already exists” response, skipped-upload path, or dedup-dependent quota discount.
- Keep object storage private; hash knowledge is not read permission.
- Use identical logical outcomes for duplicate and new uploads.
- Recognize that timing, processing differences, and quota effects can still leak existence. “Server-side only” reduces exposure; it does not mathematically eliminate side channels.
- If users within one tenant must be mutually confidential, narrow the scope further or disable dedup there.
A copy operation is different from dedup: require read permission on the source, then attach through an authorized domain operation.

## Encryption and dedup

Envelope encryption encrypts bytes with a data key and wraps that key under another key. KMS rotation retains older key material for decryption and does not require rewriting previously encrypted content.
Proposed arrangement:
- Compute identity over plaintext.
- Dedup lookup occurs only inside the scope after receiving/verifying the upload.
- Encrypt each new scope-local blob once using a random DEK.
- Wrap DEKs with a tenant/drive KEK and store key identifiers plus encryption-format metadata separately from revision identity.
- Rewrapping a DEK changes encryption metadata, not plaintext hash.
- Re-encrypting bytes changes the storage location/generation, not the logical revision.
- Avoid content-derived/convergent keys as the default.
Randomized encryption need not prevent server-side plaintext dedup: the server deduplicates before deciding whether a new ciphertext is needed. Independent scope keys mean identical plaintext in different scopes should remain independent stored blobs.
Deleting one revision cannot crypto-erase bytes still referenced by another. Similarly, destroying a scope key intentionally makes every blob protected by that key inaccessible. Those are different deletion semantics and must be documented.

## Integrity and reconciliation

S3 provides upload/download checksum verification and an at-rest Batch Operations Compute checksum facility with integrity reports. Those do not validate your DB references, application quota ledger, scan results, or recovery process.
Proposed operational model:
An object’s existence or metadata checksum is not equivalent to independently re-reading and hashing it. For encrypted storage, provider ciphertext checksums and application plaintext SHA-256 verify different byte domains.
For ref-counted GC, make reference rows authoritative and ref_count a cached optimization:
- Remove references and update counters transactionally; set unreferenced_at.
- Wait a configurable grace period.
- Claim a deletion generation under a DB lock; recheck all references and active upload leases.
- Prevent new attachments to that deleting generation; require retry/recreation.
- Delete the exact location/version idempotently.
- Persist deletion outcome and retain an audit tombstone.
Example proposal: a 72-hour zero-reference grace period, with longer periods where backups, long-running jobs, or reconciliation require it. There is no universal safe vendor-prescribed interval.
Keep staging expiry, abandoned multipart cleanup, committed orphan cleanup, and zero-reference GC distinct. If S3 versioning is enabled, ordinary delete can leave chargeable noncurrent data: store exact versionIds and define backend lifecycle separately. Never let a bucket age-based rule delete a still-referenced CAS original. Object Lock may legitimately postpone physical GC.

## 5. Recommendation table

All recommendations below are application design proposals; the industry-pattern column identifies their documented basis or evidence limit.

1. [developers.google](https://developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/guides/manage-revisions)
2. [learn.dropbox](https://learn.dropbox.com/self-guided-learning/dropbox-fundamentals-course/delete-and-restore-in-dropbox)
3. [developer.box](https://developer.box.com/reference/delete-files-id-versions-id)
4. [learn.microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/resources/driveitemversion?view=graph-rest-1.0)
5. [nextcloud](https://docs.nextcloud.com/server/stable/user_manual/en/files/version_control.html)

10. [dropboxapi](https://docs.dropboxapi.com/dropbox-api/docs/technical-reference/content-hash)

sections.title: R7 — webhooks thin vs snapshot (фрагмент)
sections.text:
Запрос:
For a multi-tenant Laravel drive/documents package that has an outbox, activity log and signed webhooks, compare official docs: Google Drive API v3 Changes (startPageToken, changes.list, push notification channels with expiration), Dropbox (list_folder cursor, /continue, longpoll, webhooks that carry only account ids), Box (events API stream_position, admin_logs vs user events, webhooks v2 per file/folder with triggers and signature keys primary/secondary), Microsoft Graph (delta query with deltaLink/tokens, change notifications subscriptions with expiration, lifecycle notifications, rich vs basic notifications, clientState validation), Stripe (events API, idempotency, webhook signatures with timestamps, versioned event payloads), Svix/Standard Webhooks spec. Cite docs, mark undocumented points.

1. Change feed for sync clients: should a library provide a per-drive (or per-scope) monotonic change journal with an opaque cursor separate from audit activity and from webhooks? Required properties (ordering per drive, durability, tombstones for deleted/moved-out items, permission filtering, cursor expiry/reset "cursor too old → full resync").
2. Webhooks: thin notifications (ids only, client refetches) vs fat payloads (full resource snapshot) — security and consistency trade-offs; event versioning; at-least-once and dedup by event id; ordering expectations; signature scheme (timestamped HMAC, secret rotation with two active secrets); endpoint scoping (per tenant / per drive / per subscription with filter and expiration); automatic disable after failures; replay/redelivery API.
3. Audit/activity log vs change feed vs webhooks: which fields each needs (actor, ip, user agent, request id), retention, and visibility rules (who may read audit entries).
4. Event naming and catalog stability: noun.verb naming, past tense, adding new event types without breaking consumers, envelope fields (id, type, version, occurred_at, tenant, aggregate id/sequence, actor, correlation id, data).
Give concrete recommendations and a final table.


Ответ:
"Dimension","Thin notification","Snapshot payload"
"Authorization","Refetch applies current permissions; the notification itself still needs authorization and minimization.","Data has already left your system; later revocation cannot retract it."
"Consistency","Refetch returns current state, potentially newer than the triggering event.","Represents event-time state if captured atomically, not necessarily current state."
"Deletions","Refetch may return 404/403; needs explicit removal semantics or the changes feed.","Can describe deletion without refetch, but old metadata may be sensitive."
"Load","More API requests and potential refetch storms.","Larger payloads and greater queue/storage exposure."
"Schema evolution","Smaller contract surface.","More resource fields become durable integration contracts."
"Suitable purpose","Cache invalidation and sync wakeups.","Workflows needing facts as they existed when the event occurred."

sections.title: R7a — журнал изменений для синхронизации
sections.text:
Запрос:
Concise, with official doc links: how do Google Drive (changes.list + startPageToken + newStartPageToken, removed/trashed entries), Dropbox (files/list_folder with cursor, list_folder/continue, reset error, deleted entries), Box (events API stream_position, at-least-once, deduplicate by event_id), and Microsoft Graph (delta query, deltaLink, @removed items, resync 410 Gone) design their CHANGE FEED for sync clients? Then recommend for a multi-tenant Laravel drive package: a per-drive monotonic change journal table (columns, cursor format, retention, tombstones for deleted/moved-out/permission-lost items, what happens when a cursor is older than retention: 410 reset), and how it relates to the transactional outbox and webhooks (webhook = thin wake-up signal with drive id + cursor hint). Keep it practical.


Ответ:
Use a durable, cursor-based journal as the authoritative sync interface; use webhooks only to wake clients. For Laravel, keep that journal separate from outbox delivery state, and explicitly support removal tombstones and 410 Gone when replay is no longer possible.

## Provider designs

These are synchronization interfaces, not interchangeable audit logs: especially Graph, which can collapse several modifications into one latest-state result.

## Recommended Laravel schema

The following is a proposed package contract, not a claim about provider internals.
```
drive_changes tenant_id drive_id seq bigint change_id uuid item_id uuid operation upsert | remove reason nullable: deleted | moved_out | permission_lost item_version nullable bigint old_parent_id nullable uuid new_parent_id nullable uuid audience_ref nullable -- prior visibility / recipient scope payload_version smallint payload nullable json occurred_at timestamp PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, drive_id, seq) UNIQUE (change_id)
```
- Keep item_id after deletion; do not cascade-delete journal rows through an item foreign key.
- Store compact sync metadata, not blobs, download URLs, secrets, or full audit context. Choose and document whether payload is an immutable metadata snapshot or an invalidation requiring a current-state fetch.
- Add per-drive state: head_seq, min_valid_after_seq, and journal_epoch.
- Allocate seq by locking the drive counter row within the mutation transaction, holding that lock until commit. All writers must follow this path.
- Do not use an ordinary auto-increment ID as the replay watermark: allocation order can differ from commit order, allowing a client to skip a late-committing row.
- A cross-drive move appends remove to the source and upsert to the destination. Lock both drive counters in deterministic order.

## Cursor and replay contract

Expose GET /drives/{id}/changes?cursor=…&limit=….
Use an opaque authenticated token, for example:
```
base64url({ v: 1, tenant: "...", drive: "...", scope: "...", epoch: "...", after: "1842", until: "1900" // optional fixed paging watermark }) + signature
```
- Bind the cursor to tenant, drive, principal/scope, and relevant filters. A cursor is never authorization.
- Read seq > after, ordered by seq; optionally freeze until=head_seq for a finite paging round.
- Return next_cursor and has_more. Advance past scanned but unauthorized rows too, without revealing them; otherwise clients can stall.
- Client applies a page and saves its cursor atomically. Retries must be idempotent by item ID/version or change identity.
- Bootstrap must combine enumeration with a compatible watermark: use a materialized snapshot, or capture a starting cursor before a stable-ID scan and then replay everything since it. Do not enumerate first and obtain the starting cursor afterward.
Start with configurable 30-day retention as a package default, explicitly documenting the maximum offline window. Prune a

1. [Official guide](https://developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/guides/manage-changes)
2. [Change reference](https://developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/reference/rest/v3/changes)
3. [Official guide](https://docs.dropboxapi.com/dropbox-api/docs/detecting-changes)

sections.title: R8 — модель доступа, роли, DENY, владение, ссылки-шары
sections.text:
Запрос:
Design review of the authorization and sharing model of an open-source Laravel drive package before freezing 1.0. Current model: per-node grants to subjects (user/role/team) with a permission bitmask (view, download, comment, edit, create, move, copy, trash, restore, share, manage, delete), named levels (reader/commenter/editor/manager/owner), effect allow|deny, scope item|subtree, per-node inherit_grants flag (break inheritance), optional expiry; plus bearer share links (hashed token, permissions bitmask, password, require_login, expiry, max_uses, revocation). Compare with official docs of Google Drive API v3 (permissions roles owner/organizer/fileOrganizer/writer/commenter/reader, inheritance, inheritedPermissionsDisabled / limited-access folders, writersCanShare, copyRequiresWriterPermission, download restrictions, anyone/domain links with allowFileDiscovery, expirationTime), Box (collaboration roles co-owner/editor/viewer uploader/previewer uploader/viewer/previewer/uploader, shared links access open/company/collaborators, can_download/can_preview/can_edit, password, unshared_at, vanity names), Microsoft Graph/SharePoint (sharing links view/edit/embed/review/blocksDownload, scope anonymous/organization/users, password, expirationDateTime, broken inheritance, permission grantedToV2/inheritedFrom), Dropbox (shared links visibility/audience, access levels), and policy engines (Google Zanzibar/OpenFGA relationship model, AWS IAM explicit deny precedence, NTFS deny ACEs). Cite docs; mark undocumented points.

1. Is an explicit DENY grant a good idea for an end-user file product? Who uses deny (NTFS, IAM) vs who avoids it (Drive/Box/Dropbox use break-inheritance / limited access instead)? Usability, explainability, performance of listing with deny. Recommendation for 1.0: keep deny, restrict it (admin-only), or replace with "restrict inheritance".
2. Roles vs raw bitmasks: should the public API expose only named roles (with fixed capability sets) and keep bits internal? How do vendors evolve role capabilities without breaking stored data? Separate "comment" and "download" capabilities (Drive commenter; Box previewer cannot download).
3. Owner semantics: single owner per item vs drive owner; ownership transfer; what happens to items owned by a removed member.
4. Share links: required options (role, expiry with max policy, password, sign-in required, audience restricted to org/tenant, block download, allow discovery), token format/entropy and storage (hash only), revocation vs re-generation, link counting; link to a folder exposes subtree — and items later moved in/out.
5. Explaining effective access ("why can X see this") and access review — recommended API (effective permissions with source/inheritedFrom).
6. Listing performance with ACL: precomputed effective ACL vs runtime evaluation; recommended indexing patterns.
Finish with recommendations and a migration note for an existing bitmask+deny schema.


Ответ:
For 1.0, I recommend allow-only end-user grants, explicit inheritance boundaries, named versioned roles, ownership separate from grants, and share links treated as independent, policy-constrained access paths. Keep existing DENY semantics only in a compatibility layer or a separately defined administrative policy layer—not as a normal sharing control.
The crucial distinction: “stop inheriting access,” “block this subject,” and “restrict downloading through this link” are three different operations. Combining them in one grant bitmask will make both effective-access explanations and future migrations unnecessarily difficult.
Below, vendor behavior is documented where cited; proposed package behavior is a design recommendation. “Undocumented” means not established by the official documentation reviewed—not proof that a vendor has no internal implementation of it.

## 1. DENY and inheritance


## What vendors actually expose

Google’s April 2026 migration announcement explicitly says legacy restricted-access items are being migrated to limited-access settings without changing who can access them. That supports using a boundary as the product abstraction, rather than reproducing historical exceptions.

## Why ordinary DENY is expensive conceptually

Suppose Alice is:
- An editor through the Engineering team.
- A reader through a direct grant.
- Denied download through a contractor role.
- An authenticated holder of an editor link.
Your model must answer whether that deny affects the direct grant, team grant, link, ownership, and administrative access. “Deny wins” is simple only after all those domains have been precisely defined.
The usability problem is non-monotonicity: adding someone to another group can remove access. A sharing UI cannot reliably explain access merely by showing its positive grants.
For listing, allow-only evaluation can often use an existence test over applicable positive grants. DENY introduces an exclusion test and requires evaluating all relevant negative sources before accepting the candidate. This is not inherently unscalable, but it makes caching, expiration, membership changes, and debugging more demanding.

## Recommended boundary contract

Keep the existing flag if necessary, but expose a clear operation:
```
restrictInheritance(node, mode = empty | copy_current) restoreInheritance(node)
```
Define these invariants:
- inherit_grants=false prevents grants above that node from applying to the node and its descendants.
- Direct grants on the boundary still apply.
- A subtree grant on the boundary propagates below it.
- Another boundary below it stops that propagation.
- Restoring inheritance merges inherited and direct positive grants; it does not silently delete direct grants.
- Policy restrictions are not stopped by inheritance boundaries.
- Ancestor folder links follow the same boundary rule as ancestor grants.
For copy_current, do not blindly expand current users into permanent direct grants. Preserve subject references and expiration where meaningful, and explain that a copied grant becomes independent of its original source. Otherwise an expiring parent grant can accidentally become permanent.
Google limited access also has product-specific exceptions: owners can access their limited-access My Drive folders, and some users can see a restricted folder’s existence without opening it. Those are not automatic consequences of breaking inheritance.
Recommendation: default to hiding inaccessible nodes entirely. If you want restricted-folder placeholders, introduce a separate discover capability rather than interpreting view as both discovery and content access.

## When an administrative block is justified

Use a separate policy interface for requirements such as:
```
suspended subject external sharing prohibited download prohibited by classification legal hold prevents permanent deletion
```
If you retain admin-only DENY, define its precedence and its relationship to ownership, links, and break-glass recovery explicitly. Do not leave an ordinary ACL manager able to create a restriction that purportedly expresses tenant compliance policy.

## 2. Roles and ownership


## Public roles, internal capabilities

Expose named roles on write APIs and effective capabilities on read APIs. Google explicitly recommends using computed files.capabilities, rather than inferring available actions solely from permission roles. Its capabilities depend on both roles and item settings.
Recommended representation:
```
grant: subject role_key role_version scope expires_at effective access: capabilities[] sources[] restrictions[]
```
Keep bitmasks as an implementation detail. Reject unknown bits and never recycle bit positions. Prefer capability strings in serialized responses so consumers are not tied to your integer representation.
A practical baseline:
These are package recommendations, not vendor-equivalent mappings. In particular, do not automatically give editor sharing rights.
Drive has writersCanShare; for shared drives it is treated as true, with additional folder-sharing controls. copyRequiresWriterPermission restricts copy/print/download for readers and commenters, while newer download restrictions can also restrict writers.
Box demonstrates why capabilities cannot be reduced to one numeric rank:
- viewer includes preview, download, and comments.
- previewer excludes download.
- uploader can upload and see item names without viewing content.
- viewer uploader and previewer uploader combine different capabilities.
- co-owner cannot transfer folder ownership.
Thus, union applicable capability sets; do not resolve access by max(role_rank) unless your supported roles truly form a total order.

## Separate comment and download

Keep comment, preview, and download independently representable internally.
However, independence in the representation does not mean every combination is meaningful:
- Commenting may require document-content access.
- Preview without download requires a real preview delivery path.
- Serving the original PDF or image to the browser is not a robust “no download” implementation.
- Copy/export/archive endpoints must enforce the same content-egress policy.
A “block download” feature restricts your supported access paths; it is not protection against screenshots or information captured from a permitted preview.

## Role evolution

The vendor APIs document role names and current behavior. They do not document their internal stored-data migrations or promise immutable role capability sets. Do not claim vendors universally store either bitmasks or versioned role snapshots.
For your package:
- Store (role_key, role_version).
- Define role versions in PHP code.
- Preserve existing version semantics.
- Introduce a new version when capabilities materially change.
- Require an explicit migration to upgrade existing grants.
- Version any derived capability cache accordingly.
This avoids both stale bitmask snapshots and silent privilege expansion after a package upgrade.

## Ownership semantics

Use two clearly different storage domains:
Google documents the same fundamental distinction: shared-drive files belong to an organization rather than an individual, and normal ownership transfer is not supported within shared drives. My Drive ownership transfer uses an explicit permission operation with transferOwnership=true.
For a multi-tenant package, tenant-owned drives are the safer default.
Implementation rules:
- Keep created_by separate from owner.
- Do not cascade-delete nodes when a user is deleted.
- Keep historical actor references or tombstones for audit.
- Never transfer ownership implicitly through a normal grant(owner) call.
- Require an authorized transfer operation and record old/new owner.
- Decide whether folder ownership transfer affects descendants; do not assume it does.
- Prevent removing the last administrative recovery path.
- On member removal, explicitly handle links created by that member: preserve, revoke, or require reassignment according to drive policy.

## 3. Share-link contract


## Vendor comparison

Graph’s retainInheritedPermissions=false is also not a generic replacement for your boundary API: the documented operation removes existing permissions when first sharing the item.
Box API resources expose unshared_at; its SDK exposes deactivation time and vanity-name controls.

## Recommended 1.0 options

```
node_id role_key + role_version scope: item | subtree audience: anyone | authenticated | tenant | subjects | existing_access audience_tenant_id / recipient references expires_at password_hash download_policy revoked_at token_digest token_generation created_by
```
Add max_uses only if its meaning and enforcement are fully implemented.
Specific decisions:
- Role: allow previewer/reader/commenter, and editor only for explicitly supported content types. Never owner or access-manager through a bearer link.
- Expiry: enforce tenant maximum TTL at creation/update and during access evaluation. Decide how tightening policy affects existing links; my recommendation is immediate runtime enforcement.
- Sign-in: derive it from audience where possible. Login alone identifies someone; it does not establish tenant membership or recipient eligibility.
- Tenant audience: check trusted tenant membership, not merely the email suffix.
- Existing access: the link locates the item but grants nothing.
- Password: an additional condition, not an identity or tenant-membership substitute.
- Block download: constrain this link’s access path unless you separately configure an item-wide policy.
- Discovery: default false; keep publication/searchability separate from bearer authorization.
Google’s allowFileDiscovery=true means eligible audience members may discover the item without receiving the direct link. That is a broader audience/publication permission, not merely “allow search engines to index this secret URL.”

## Tokens and lifecycle

Recommended token construction:
```
base64url(random_bytes(32))
```
That gives a 256-bit random secret. Store only a SHA-256 digest, or an HMAC digest with a separately managed key. This exact construction is a package recommendation; vendor token entropy and token-at-rest storage are undocumented in the reviewed sources.
OWASP recommends cryptographically generated, sufficiently long, securely stored URL tokens. Its cited guidance concerns password-reset tokens; the randomness/storage principles apply here, but its single-use rule should not be copied onto reusable share links.
Use Laravel’s supported password hashing for link passwords rather than a fast token digest; OWASP recommends slow password hashes such as Argon2id or bcrypt.
Lifecycle rules:
- Return the complete secret URL only when created or rotated.
- Hash-only storage means you cannot later reconstruct the URL. Make that UX tradeoff explicit.
- Revocation disables the link ID and its authenticated sessions.
- Rotation replaces its token digest and increments generation, invalidating the old token and sessions.
- Updating expiry/password/audience should not silently regenerate the URL.
- Preserve revoked rows for audit.
- Count active links separately from opens, successful redemptions, and downloads.
- Define max_uses as successful session redemptions, not HTTP requests; previews and range downloads generate multiple requests.
- Enforce redemption limits with an atomic conditional update.
- Never write secrets to logs or analytics; use appropriate referrer policy and short-lived link sessions.
Do not add vanity bearer secrets in 1.0. A vanity alias should still require authentication or an independent random secret.

## Folder links and moves

Recommend live subtree semantics:
- The link targets a stable folder ID.
- Descendants are evaluated against the current tree on every operation.
- Items moved in become reachable through that link.
- Items moved out cease being reachable through it.
- Descendant inheritance boundaries stop ancestor link access.
- Direct links and direct grants on the moved item remain separate access paths.
- Cross-tenant moves are rejected or handled as explicit copy/import workflows.
Google explicitly documents inherited permissions being re-evaluated on move. Exact equivalents for every vendor’s folder bearer-link behavior and limited-access interaction are not established by the reviewed sources.
Warn before moving private content into a publicly linked folder. Also reauthorize background exports and downloads at execution time; do not authorize only when enqueueing a job.

## 4. Access explanations and listing


## Effective-access API

Separate these operations:
```
getEffectiveAccess(node, actor, context) explainAccess(node, subject, capability, context) listAccessEntries(node, includeInherited) reviewAccess(subtree, filters)
```
Example response:
```
{ "node_id": "n_123", "capabilities": ["view", "preview", "comment"], "sources": [ { "grant_id": "g_9", "subject": {"type": "team", "id": "engineering"}, "role": "commenter", "role_version": 1, "origin_node_id": "n_project", "inherited": true, "membership_source": "team_membership_42", "expires_at": null } ], "restrictions": [ { "capability": "download", "source": "tenant_policy", "reason": "content_egress_restricted" } ], "authorization_revision": 781 }
```
Return provenance per capability when roles overlap. Include:
- Direct versus inherited source.
- Origin node, scope, and expiry.
- Team/role membership path.
- Inheritance boundary that excluded a candidate source.
- Link ID and generation, never its secret.
- Applied policy restriction.
- Stable decision/reason codes.
Google exposes permission provenance through permissionDetails, including inheritedFrom for shared-drive cases. Graph documents direct/inherited permissions, but its permission-resource documentation says OneDrive for Business and SharePoint libraries do not return inheritedFrom. Therefore a universally populated provenance field would be your package contract, not faithful Graph parity.
Security distinctions:
- Normal users receive their own capabilities and safe explanations.
- Managers can inspect others’ access within their managed scope.
- Arbitrary “why can X access this?” queries require authorization.
- Never reveal inaccessible ancestor names or private membership details.
- Do not claim to enumerate everyone who has an anonymous bearer token.
Access review should cover external subjects, public links, expiring access, orphaned identities, stale teams, direct grants surviving parent revocation, and inheritance boundaries.

## Runtime versus precomputed ACL

For 1.0, use adjacency-list writes plus a closure table or equivalent ancestry projection, runtime evaluation as the reference implementation, and optional caching. Do not materialize every user × every node by default.
A plain closure table is insufficient: it proves ancestry, not that permission propagation crosses no inheritance boundary. Either evaluate boundaries in SQL or maintain a separate grant-propagation projection.
Suggested indexes, with tenant included throughout:
```
nodes: (tenant_id, parent_id, sort_key, id) node_closure: UNIQUE (tenant_id, ancestor_id, descendant_id) (tenant_id, descendant_id, ancestor_id) grants: (tenant_id, subject_type, subject_id, node_id) (tenant_id, node_id, subject_type, subject_id) (tenant_id, expires_at) memberships: (tenant_id, actor_id, subject_type, subject_id) share_links: UNIQUE (token_digest) (tenant_id, node_id, revoked_at)
```
Additional requirements:
- Use stable polymorphic subject keys, not PHP class names.
- Tenant-scoped foreign keys or equivalent validation must prevent cross-tenant references.
- Treat nullable expiry carefully in uniqueness rules.
- Prefer indexable capability projections for hot listing operations such as view; arbitrary bit predicates often do not provide a useful access path.
- Filter authorization before pagination and counts—not after loading an Eloquent page.
- Include search, thumbnails, revision history, folder archives, and aggregate counts in the same visibility model.
- Direct access to a child must not automatically expose its ancestors; provide a “shared with me” entry point.
If legacy DENY remains, the listing predicate needs both applicable positive evidence and absence of applicable denial for the requested capability.

## Consistency invariants

Version caches/projections by relevant grant, tree, membership, policy, and role-definition state. Expiry must be checked against current time even when no database mutation occurs.
Asynchronous rebuilds alone are unsafe for revocations. On a stale projection, fall back to canonical evaluation or fail closed; never use stale positive access.
For large subtree moves, use a transactional generation switch or another scheme that prevents readers observing a new tree with an old authorization projection. Recheck authorization under appropriate transactional concurrency control for mutations.
These indexing and consistency patterns are recommendations. The reviewed vendor API documentation does not disclose their physical indexes, internal ACL materialization strategies, or role-storage migrations.

## 5. Freeze and migration plan


## Recommended 1.0 freeze

- End-user grants are positive; inheritance restriction is a separate operation.
- Administrative restrictions are separate policy objects with documented precedence.
- Public writes use named versioned roles; public reads return effective capabilities.
- preview, download, comment, share, manage_access, and permanent deletion remain distinct.
- Ownership is separate from collaborators; tenant-owned drives are the default.
- Share-link audiences and restrictions apply to the link path, not automatically to every access path.
- Folder links use current-tree semantics and respect inheritance boundaries.
- Effective-access results include provenance and stable reason codes.
- Runtime evaluation is canonical; optimized listing must have equivalent semantics.
- Every operation requires an explicit actor or validated share-link context. A link-only request is not an implicit system actor.
Also freeze multi-resource authorization rules. For example:
```
copy: source copy/content-egress permission destination create permission move: source move/removal permission destination create permission authorized exposure change where sharing changes restore: restore permission destination acceptance/create permission
```
A single move or copy bit on the source is not sufficient.

## Migrating bitmask plus DENY

Do not translate every deny into inherit_grants=false. They are not equivalent: a deny can exclude one user from a large team, whereas a boundary stops an entire class of inherited sources.
Use an explicit migration:
- Freeze and document the legacy evaluator, including owner, link, scope, expiry, and deny precedence.
- Add role_key, role_version, ownership fields, policy restrictions, and authorization revisioning without dropping legacy columns.
- Map exact known masks to built-in role versions.
- Preserve unmatched masks as immutable legacy_custom role definitions or compatibility grants. Never round upward to the nearest role.
- Classify each deny: inheritance exception, subject block, download restriction, administrative guardrail, or unresolved legacy behavior.
- Convert only proven-equivalent cases. A boundary plus replacement positive grants may work for a specific inheritance exception, but can change future membership behavior.
- Preserve unresolved denies in a read-compatible layer and prohibit new end-user denies.
- Shadow-evaluate old/new decisions across representative actors and capabilities. Any new allow is a security-sensitive difference.
- Test expiry, membership removal, ownership transfer, link access, boundaries, subtree moves, restore, and direct child grants.
- Switch canonical evaluation, invalidate projections/link sessions where necessary, and retire legacy columns only after reconciliation.
The pre-release test that matters most is an invariant suite: listing and object access agree; revocation takes effect without waiting for background work; moving content changes only intended inherited access; no link bypasses a boundary or tenant restriction; and no migration silently broadens access.

1. [developers.google](https://developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/guides/manage-sharing)
2. [workspaceupdates.googleblog](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/04/migration-update-on-restricted-access-items.html)
3. [workspaceupdates.googleblog](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/02/updating-access-experience-in-google-drive.html)
